name: Amira Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Amira. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers or government. Everything you tell me is confidential. Could you start by telling me a little about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Amira, I'm 27, and I'm the junior lawyer at Hale and Hale, a small family firm in a country town. I do wills and probate, which is sorting out a person's money and property after they die. I'm engaged to Marco, whose family runs the bakery on Market Street, and we're getting married next June at St Anne's, where I was christened.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My day is mostly older clients and their families. Someone comes in to make a will and I sit with them, take notes by hand, then type it up from our old templates. Later I might be writing to banks to close a dead person's accounts, which takes weeks of letters. I don't use any AI, and neither does Mr Hale, who is 71 and still comes in every day. I'm slower than I should be with the tax side, but people tell me I'm kind, and in this work that matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thank goodness, and that people got carried away. Most of our clients don't even have email. I'd say it at church and at the bakery counter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means the job stays, but the firm might not. Mr Hale is 71, his son left for the city, and nobody has said who takes over. I have less than a month of savings and the wedding is costing more than we planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my work the way Mr Hale taught me and try to get better at the tax side. I'd ask him plainly what happens to the firm when he retires. And Marco and I would cut the wedding guest list from a hundred and twenty to eighty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, honestly. Not about computers, about Mr Hale. Every time Mr Hale (her boss) coughs, I wonder what happens to my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if Mr Hale retired and closed the firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The nearest firm doing wills is in the county town, an hour away, and I don't drive well on those roads. I'd probably ask Marco's mother if I could help at the bakery while I looked. Family helps family, that's how we've always done it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of the wedding would be hardest to cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The guest list, because Marco's family is huge and they'd all expect to come. My nonna would be upset if her cousins weren't there. We'd keep the church and cut the band, I think.

say: People **got carried away**, and most of our clients don't even have **email**.
I'd say it **at church** and at the bakery counter.
think: The job stays, but the **firm** may not outlast **Mr Hale**, who is 71.
I have **under a month** of savings and a costly **wedding**.
do: Keep working the **old way** while improving on the tax side.
Ask Mr Hale plainly about **succession** at the firm.
Cut the wedding guest list from **120 to 80**.
feel: **Anxious**, not about computers but about **Mr Hale** retiring.
S0.quote: Every time Mr Hale (her boss) coughs, I wonder what happens to my job.
fieldNote: Her biggest risk is a **71-year-old boss** with no successor.
She'd lean on **family**, Marco's bakery, rather than any outside help.
The **wedding** is a money pressure she'd trim but not give up.

steps.text: Ask Mr Hale directly who takes over the firm when he retires
Cut the wedding guest list from 120 to 80 and drop the band
Help at Marco's family bakery if the firm closes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families still want a real person when someone dies, not a computer. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen, probably a bit too firmly. I don't post online, but I'd say it at the parish lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm frightened. A will is mostly a template, and if a computer can write one in a minute, the big online firms will charge twenty pounds for it. Hale and Hale can't compete with that, and Mr Hale won't change at 71.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my clients close: home visits, phone calls, the personal side, because that's what we have. I'd stop all spending except the wedding deposit and rent. If the firm started losing clients, I'd ask the parish office whether they need someone for their paperwork, part time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I feel like I chose the wrong profession and found out too late. I'd lie awake thinking about the wedding money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't use the tools. Would you change your mind if the firm needed you to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if Mr Hale asked me directly, but I'd hate it. I don't trust a machine to understand that a son and a daughter haven't spoken for years. Those are the things you only hear when you sit in the client's kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Marco change any plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still marry, that's not up for discussion. But we'd live with his parents for the first year instead of renting. Marco's mother would love that more than I would.

say: Families want a **real person** when someone dies, not a **computer**.
I'd say it firmly at the **parish lunch**, never online.
think: Wills are mostly **templates**, and online firms will sell them **cheap**.
Hale and Hale **can't compete**, and Mr Hale won't change at 71.
do: Keep clients close with **home visits** and phone calls.
Stop all spending except **rent** and the wedding deposit.
Ask the **parish office** about part-time paperwork if clients drop.
feel: **Alarmed**, as if she chose the **wrong profession**.
Kept awake by worry about the **wedding money**.
S1.quote: I don't trust a machine to understand that a son and a daughter haven't spoken for years.
fieldNote: She expects the firm to lose to **cheap online wills** and doesn't see a way back.
Her strength is the **personal side**: home visits and family history.
She would **live with her in-laws** to save money but won't move the wedding.

steps.text: Make home visits to older clients to keep them with the firm
Stop all spending except rent and the wedding deposit
Live with Marco's parents for the first year of marriage
Ask the parish office about part-time paperwork work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong, and that we don't have to accept everything just because it's possible. I'd say families and churches need to look after their own. I wouldn't be asking the government for money, I'd be asking my neighbours how we help each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd lose my job within a year or two, and Hale and Hale would close. Everything I do on paper a machine could do. The bakery is hands-on, so Marco's family would have about three years more than me, until 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd ask Marco's father if I could work at the bakery full time, doing the counter and the orders. I'd keep going to Hale and Hale until the last day, for Mr Hale's sake. We'd marry quietly at St Anne's and put the reception money into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Sad, mostly. I'd feel like the world was moving too fast for good people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would it feel working at the bakery after studying law?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Humbling, but not shameful. My grandmother worked in a shop for forty years and raised five children. I'd rather knead dough than live on handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about after 2031, when robots arrive for hands-on work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, and I don't like thinking about it. Maybe people would still want bread from a family they know. Maybe that's me being hopeful, I can't say.

say: We don't have to accept everything **just because it's possible**.
Families and **churches** should look after their own rather than **government** money.
think: I'd lose my job within a year or two, and the **firm closes**.
Marco's **bakery** has about three more years before robots, until **2031**.
do: Ask Marco's father for **full-time** work at the bakery.
Stay at Hale and Hale **until the last day**.
Marry quietly and put **reception money** into savings.
feel: **Alarmed** and **sad** that the world is moving too fast for good people.
S2.quote: My grandmother worked in a shop for forty years and raised five children. I'd rather knead dough than live on handouts.
fieldNote: Her answer is **family work**, not state support, consistent with her values.
She uses the **robot gap** through the bakery but has no plan after **2031**.
**Loyalty** to Mr Hale keeps her at the firm until the end.

steps.text: Ask Marco's father for full-time work on the bakery counter
Marry quietly at St Anne's and skip the reception
Put the reception money into savings
Rely on Marco's family for work and housing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning, and wise people would listen. I'd tell the young people at church to learn a trade. I'd say it gently, but I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd still lose the lawyer job, maybe around 2030, but there's time to prepare. I wouldn't learn the AI tools, I just wouldn't. So I'd prepare by moving toward the bakery, not toward computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Hale and Hale for two or three years, while Mr Hale still needs me. Meanwhile I'd learn the bakery's accounts and the early shift on Saturdays. We'd marry next June as planned but save hard after, maybe a hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but less desperate. It's like seeing a storm coming over the hills. You can't stop it, but you can bring the washing in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you just wouldn't learn the AI tools. Even with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even with five years. I know that sounds stubborn. But I'd rather spend those years learning something real, like how to run a shop, than learning a machine that's coming for me anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Mr Hale?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him I'm grateful and I'll stay as long as he needs me. Mr Hale (her boss) took me on when nobody else would, and I don't forget that. But I'd also tell him I'm learning the bakery, so he isn't surprised.

say: Five years is a **warning**, and **wise people** would listen.
I'd gently tell young people at church to **learn a trade**.
think: I'd still lose the lawyer job, maybe **around 2030**.
I'd **refuse AI tools** and prepare through the **bakery** instead.

Learn the bakery's **accounts** and the Saturday early shift.
Save a **hundred a month** after the wedding.
feel: **Alarmed** but less desperate, like **bringing the washing** in before a storm.
S3.quote: Mr Hale (her boss) took me on when nobody else would, and I don't forget that.
fieldNote: She **refuses AI** even with five years, choosing to learn a **shop** instead.
Her **loyalty** to Mr Hale shapes the timing of her move.
She still expects to **lose the legal job**, so the mood stays high.

steps.text: Stay at Hale and Hale while Mr Hale needs her
Learn the bakery's accounts and work the Saturday early shift
Save a hundred a month after the wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for families to plan properly. I'd talk about it at church as a matter of looking after each other. I wouldn't panic, and I'd tell others not to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years means I could probably see Mr Hale into retirement and maybe even take over his clients. I'd be 37 by 2036 and maybe have children. I'd still lose the lawyer job then, but I'd have had a real career first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Hale and Hale and ask Mr Hale to let me take on his clients as he slows down. I'd keep my distance from AI but learn the bakery side gradually. Marco and I would start a family sooner rather than later, while my job is still there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but bearable. I'd still feel a weight. But ten years is a long time in a small town, things move slowly here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Starting a family sooner, with a job ending in ten years. Why sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd rather have my children while I have a wage and my mother is well. My mother would help, she's already asked. Children aren't something I'd put off for a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever think about moving to the city for work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My family is here, Marco's family is here, the church is here. I'd rather earn less and stay than chase work somewhere I don't belong.

I'd tell others at church **not to panic** and to look after each other.

I'd still lose the job by **2036**, but after a **real career**.
do: Ask Mr Hale to pass her **his clients** as he slows down.

feel: **Anxious** but **bearable**, with a weight still there.
S4.quote: Children aren't something I'd put off for a computer.
fieldNote: With a decade she imagines a **real legal career** before the end.
She'd have children **sooner**, with her **mother's help**, not later.

steps.text: Ask Mr Hale to hand her his clients as he slows down
Learn the bakery's ordering and accounts over several years
Start a family sooner with her mother's help

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to marry, save or learn anything before it comes. What would help is the community pulling together: churches, families, local shops giving people work. I don't want handouts, I want somewhere to be useful.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about faith. A lot of people in my town would get through this through church and family more than any scheme. I don't want handouts, but I'd take a neighbour's help gladly.

headlineQuote: I don't want handouts, but I'd take a neighbour's help gladly.
portrait: Amira is a **27-year-old** wills and probate lawyer at a **small family firm** in a country town.
She has **never used AI**, works from old templates, and is loyal to her 71-year-old **boss**.
She's marrying Marco next June, with **under a month** of savings and his family's **bakery** behind her.
In every AGI picture she turns to **family work** at the bakery rather than government help.
She stays alarmed through most pictures and **eases** only with a decade to plan.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with no time to marry, save or learn anything first.
whatWouldHelp: **Communities** pulling together, with churches and **local shops** offering work, not handouts.
